title: Kirat karo, deeper
hookLine: honest work as spiritual practice, not only income

cards: Sawdust on the forearms. A plane sliding along a board, curls of wood dropping to the floor.
Somewhere in Punjab, the story goes, a carpenter named Lalo worked like this all day, while a rich official named Malik Bhago threw a great feast down the road. Guru Nanak was invited to the feast.
He ate the carpenter's plain bread instead. When the official demanded to know why, the story says, Nanak took bread from each table and squeezed. From Lalo's came milk.
From the feast came blood. It's a story Sikhs tell, not a line from the Granth. But it asks today's question: what is the work of your hands made of?

teach.b: One Sikh summary of Guru Nanak's way has three short phrases: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn by honest work; vand chhako, share what you have.
This path met them before; this week each gets a deeper day, starting with work.

teach.h: KIRAT: THE WORK OF YOUR OWN EFFORT.
teach.b: Kirat means labor, the work of your own effort. Karo means do it. Under it sits a salok of Guru Nanak, in paraphrase: someone who calls himself a guru or a holy man and goes about begging, don't bow at his feet.

teach.h: EARN, AND GIVE FROM THE HAND.
teach.b: The one who eats what he has earned by his own effort, and gives some of it from his hand, Nanak says, that one recognizes the path. Holiness isn't proven by leaving work behind.
In this line, the one who has found the way has a paycheck, a harvest or a till, and something in their hand to give. Earning and the path aren't two rooms. They're the same room.
That's why the Lalo story lands. It isn't against wealth; it's about where the bread came from. Bread made by honest hands carries something good.
Bread made by squeezing other people carries what was squeezed. So kirat is more than having a job.

It's how the job is done: the honest invoice, the full hour for the full wage, the repair done right when nobody would notice. Done that way, the work becomes part of the practice, not a break from it.
That's today's line: work as prayer.

how: Sikhs speak of kirat karo as earning a living honestly by their own effort, and Sikh teachers describe daily work, done truthfully, as part of a Sikh life rather than apart from it.

o: give up work and live on what others offer
earn your living by honest work of your own effort
work hard now so you can retire early to pray

games.q: the three phrases: tap the pairs.
p: the carpenter whose bread Nanak ate

s: in the salok, the one who gives up work and begs is the holy one
the salok says don't bow to the self-styled holy man who begs; the one who earns and gives recognizes the path.
the milk-and-blood bread is a story Sikhs tell, not a line in the Granth
it's a story about Lalo and Malik Bhago; the Granth line is the salok about earning and giving.
kirat karo is only about having a job
it's about how the work is done: honestly, by your own effort, with something to give.

games.q: a carpenter offers plain bread. a rich official offers a feast. you are Guru Nanak. where do you eat?
o: at the feast, to honor the official.
games.why: the story says he ate Lalo's bread, and when pressed, showed milk in it and blood in the feast's.

practice: Choose one hour ahead, your job, cooking, cleaning, study, caring for someone, and set one intention for it: honest, whole, done well, nobody watching required.
Rest your hands open on your knees, the hands that will do the work, and breathe slowly. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Kirat karo. Earn by honest work, the labor of your own effort, done in a way that is itself part of the spiritual life. Today's word.

orig.note: kirat is labor, the work of your own effort; karo means do it.

carryVoice: Your line: work as prayer. Lalo's plain bread was the meal Nanak chose. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Sarang ki Var, salok Mahala 1, Ang 1245 (one who eats what he earns by effort and gives something from his hand recognizes the path)
Janamsakhi tradition: Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago
